documentation.title: User Guide
documentation.description: Learn how to use CodeKB to analyze, explore, and understand your codebases.

what.title: What is CodeKB?
what.p1: CodeKB is an AI-powered code analysis system that extracts structure from your source code, builds call graphs, and enables semantic search across your entire codebase. It helps you understand how code is organized, trace execution flows, and find components by describing what they do in plain English.
what.p2: It's built for engineers ramping up on an unfamiliar service, teams doing brownfield work across many repositories, and AI coding assistants that need reliable, structured context about a codebase rather than raw file access.
what.pillMcp: Works in your editor via MCP

who.title: Who it's for and use cases
who.body: CodeKB is built for engineers ramping onto an unfamiliar codebase, teams doing brownfield work across many repositories, and AI assistants that need grounded, structured knowledge of a code base rather than raw file access. If you are joining a new service, auditing how a feature flows across repos, or wiring an IDE assistant to understand your code, CodeKB is for you.

concepts.title: Core concepts
concepts.description: Two ideas you'll see throughout the product
concepts.spacesBody: A space is a self-contained knowledge base built from one codebase. It holds the parsed component catalog, call graph, statistics, and vector embeddings. Create a space from a Git repository or a zip upload.
concepts.hyperspacesBody: A hyperspace groups one or more spaces so you can search and query across related codebases as a single unit — handy for microservice fleets or multi-repo platforms.

start.title: Getting started
start.description: Follow these steps to get up and running
start.step1Body: Go to the Spaces page and click "New space". Provide a Git repository URL (HTTPS or SSH) and optionally pick a branch or tag, or upload a zip of your source. Under Analysis options you can omit low business relevance components from AI summarization to save time and cost.
start.step2Body: Watch the live pipeline steps and summarization progress bar on the space page. CodeKB reports any files skipped because their language isn't supported yet.
start.step3Body: Open a space and use the Syntactic Search tab to find components by name, pattern, or type, or the Semantic Search tab to find them by describing what they do. From any component, view source, trace its execution flow, and inspect dependencies.
start.step4Body: Open the Space Overview tab to generate AI documentation of the codebase's architecture, components, and data flows. Regenerate it after big changes.
start.step5Body: Use Global search to run one query across all spaces, a chosen subset, or a hyperspace. Group related spaces into a hyperspace from the Hyperspaces page.
start.step6Body: For Git-sourced spaces, click "Refresh space" to run a space refresh against the latest commit.
start.step7Body: Each space shows token usage per operation with cost estimates.
start.step8Body: Open Agent Hopper from the sidebar, select one or more spaces, and ask questions in plain English. Switch to Impact Analysis mode to assess the effect of a described change.
start.step9Body: Add CodeKB as an MCP server in your AI coding assistant (Kiro, Amazon Q Developer CLI, or any MCP-compatible tool). See the MCP setup section below for the config snippet.

features.title: Key features
features.semanticBody: Find components by what they do, not just literal text, using vector search over AI-written summaries.
features.callGraphBody: Trace callers and callees across the whole code base to see how functions and components call each other.
features.overviewBody: Generates Business Overview, Application Architecture, Technology Stack, and Deployment docs for a single space.
features.hyperspaceOverviewBody: A system-level view across a hyperspace: what the whole system does, plus a map of how its member spaces connect.
features.relevanceBody: Ranks components by how likely they carry business logic, so AI summarization focuses where it matters.
features.refreshBody: Re-analyzes only the files changed since the last commit, then swaps in the new index atomically.
features.agentBodySuffix: traces the components and flows a described change would touch.
features.globalBody: Run one query across all spaces, a chosen subset, or a whole hyperspace, and rank matches across them.
features.dashboardBody: The home page aggregates metrics and renders an interactive Treemap of your spaces and hyperspaces.
features.costBody: Per-operation Bedrock token counts and cost estimates, broken down per space and per hyperspace synthesis.
features.authBody: OAuth 2.0 / OIDC sign-in via Amazon Cognito, federatable to your own IdP, plus an OAuth-protected MCP endpoint.
features.repoBody: Save a per-provider access token (GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket) to clone private repos, encrypted and scoped to you.
features.settingsBody: Shows live readiness of the S3 and Vectors buckets, the vector index, the git-credentials KMS key, the active Bedrock model and region, and which providers are enabled.
features.mcpBody: Expose search, overviews, and code tracing to IDE assistants over an OAuth-protected MCP endpoint.

access.title: Authentication and access
access.description: How people and AI assistants sign in, and how private repos are reached
access.signInBody: CodeKB authenticates users with OAuth 2.0 / OIDC through Amazon Cognito. Cognito can federate to your own identity provider, so each deployment can plug in its own corporate sign-in. Sign-in is optional and off by default when you self-host: the shipped configuration runs with authentication disabled and bound to localhost, so you turn on Cognito (the reference CDK wires it for you) or put your own identity provider in front before exposing CodeKB beyond your machine.
access.assistantBody: The MCP endpoint is OAuth-protected. Your IDE assistant runs a standard OAuth sign-in the first time it connects, handled by a built-in proxy, so you do not manage tokens by hand.
access.privateBody: Private-repo ingestion is separate from sign-in and does not use an OAuth app flow. You save a personal access token for your Git provider (GitHub by default; GitLab and Bitbucket when your deployment enables them). The token is stored encrypted, is never shown back to you, and is scoped to your account.

mcp.title: MCP and integrations
mcp.intro: After deploying CodeKB, you can connect it as an MCP server to your AI coding assistant. The server exposes tools for loading spaces, searching components, tracing flows, and running semantic queries.
mcp.configNotePrefix: Add this to your MCP client's configuration file (e.g. Kiro, Amazon Q Developer CLI, or any MCP-compatible tool). Replace
mcp.configNoteSuffix: with your deployed CodeKB URL. On an auth-enforced instance, your client completes an OAuth sign-in on first connect.
mcp.canDoBody: Once connected, the assistant can load a space, search components, trace flows, inspect dependencies, pull the call graph, and list spaces and hyperspaces. The MCP endpoint exposes these tools:

how.title: How it works
how.description: From raw source to an AI assistant that understands your codebase
how.intro: CodeKB runs as a service that sits between your source code and the people and tools that consume it. A web UI and REST API drive analysis and exploration, coding agents connect over MCP, and the knowledge base is persisted in S3 with embeddings and summaries produced by Amazon Bedrock models.
how.architectureAlt: CodeKB architecture: the CodeKB service connects the web UI (REST API), identity providers (OAuth2/SAML), and coding agents (MCP) to source inputs (Git, zip, S3) and backing stores (S3 component catalog, S3 Vectors knowledge base, and Bedrock embedding and LLM models).
how.architectureCaption: CodeKB system architecture. Some integration points are forward-looking.
how.webUiBody: Create spaces, browse components, and search — over the REST API.
how.agentsBody: Connect over MCP to query the knowledge base from your editor.
how.sourceBody: Ingested from a Git repository, a zip upload, or S3.
how.automationsBody: REST API and webhooks to keep spaces fresh from CI/CD.
how.storageBody: S3 component catalog, S3 Vectors knowledge base, and Bedrock embedding + LLM models.
how.lifecycleBody: A space moves through ANALYZING, SUMMARIZING, READY, FAILED, and REFRESHING as it is built and kept up to date.
how.workflowAlt: End-to-end CodeKB workflow: a developer analyzes a codebase in CodeKB, which ingests and parses it, summarizes functions with an LLM, vectorizes the summaries, and persists everything in S3; the developer then works in an AI coding assistant that queries LLMs and issues CodeKB MCP commands to navigate the codebase.
how.flow1: A developer uses the CodeKB UI to analyze an application codebase.
how.flow2: CodeKB ingests the codebase (Git clone, zip upload, or S3).
how.flow3: CodeKB parses the code and builds the call graph, invokes an LLM to summarize functions, and invokes an embeddings model to vectorize those summaries.
how.flow4: CodeKB persists the component catalog, a source clone, and the function-summary vectors in AWS S3.
how.flow5: The developer initiates brownfield development tasks in an AI coding assistant.
how.flow6: The AI coding assistant queries LLMs.
how.flow7: The LLM issues CodeKB MCP commands to navigate the brownfield codebase structure in a loop.

relevance.title: Business behaviour relevance
relevance.description: How CodeKB decides which components are worth deeper AI summarization
relevance.p1: Business behaviour relevance is a computational score from 0 to 100 that estimates whether a function or method represents meaningful product behaviour, workflow logic, or domain orchestration. Low-scoring components are usually framework glue, helpers, adapters, tests, generated code, or tiny technical utilities.
relevance.p2: The score is calculated after parsing and call graph creation, before AI summarization. It does not require an LLM per component. If AI summarization is enabled, CodeKB can optionally omit components in the low tier to reduce runtime and token usage.
relevance.graph1: Call depth: +8 per level, capped at +32
relevance.graph2: Fan in: +4 per caller, capped at +20
relevance.graph3: Fan out: +3 per dependency, capped at +18
relevance.business1: Generic business terms in name: +6 each, capped at +18
relevance.business2: Repository-specific business terms in name: +10 each, capped at +30
relevance.business3: Business path terms: +5 each, capped at +15
relevance.business4: Repository business modules in path: +8 each, capped at +24
relevance.business5: Repository entrypoint patterns: +30 each, capped at +40
relevance.business6: Detected domain concepts: +5 each, capped at +15
relevance.metadata3: Complexity above 1: +2 per point, capped at +12
relevance.metadata4: Implementation length of 20 lines or more: +8
relevance.metadata5: Implementation length of 3 lines or less: -10
relevance.penalties1: Generic technical terms in name: -6 each, capped at -18
relevance.penalties2: Repository-specific technical terms in name: -8 each, capped at -24
relevance.penalties3: Technical path terms: -8 each, capped at -24
relevance.p3: Final scores are clamped to the 0-100 range. CodeKB labels scores below 25 as low, 25-49.9 as heuristic, 50-79.9 as medium, and 80 or above as high. The “omit low business relevance” option skips only the low tier during AI summarization; the components still remain in the parsed catalog and call graph.

limits.title: Limits, data, and cost
limits.sizeBody: There is no hard cap. Code bases beyond 2M lines have been analyzed.
limits.exclusionsPrefix: CodeKB skips common noise such as
limits.exclusionsAuto: automatically, and you can add your own
limits.exclusionsSuffix: ). A space keeps the patterns it was created with.
limits.dataBody: The source clone, the component catalog, and the summary vectors are stored in S3 and S3 Vectors in the AWS account where CodeKB runs. That is the account that operates your deployment, and your code stays within it.
limits.costBody: CodeKB runs on Amazon Bedrock, S3, and S3 Vectors. The main cost is Bedrock LLM tokens: a one-time cost when a space is summarized, plus recurring cost for chat and queries. Embedding cost is negligible by comparison. Every space shows the tokens used for creation and for each space refresh.

faq.title: FAQ
faq.dataQ: Where does my code go, and where is my data stored?
faq.dataA: CodeKB stores the source clone, the component catalog, and the summary vectors in S3 and S3 Vectors in the AWS account where it runs. That is the account that operates your deployment, so your code stays within it.
faq.costA: CodeKB runs on Amazon Bedrock, S3, and S3 Vectors. The main cost is Bedrock LLM tokens: a one-time cost when a space is summarized, plus recurring cost for chat and queries. Embedding cost is negligible by comparison. Every space shows the tokens used for creation and for each space refresh, so you can price it against the Bedrock pricing page. Tip: enable "omit low business relevance components" to cut summarization cost.
faq.mcpQ: How do I connect my AI assistant over MCP?
faq.mcpASuffix: ) to your MCP client config (Kiro, Amazon Q Developer CLI, Claude Code). On an auth-enforced instance your client completes an OAuth sign-in on first connect. Once connected, the assistant can load a space, search components, trace flows, inspect dependencies, and pull the call graph.
faq.hyperspaceQ: What is a Hyperspace Overview, and how is it different from a Space Overview?
faq.hyperspaceA: A Space Overview documents one code base (business, architecture, tech stack, deployment). A Hyperspace Overview sits on top of a group of spaces and produces two system-level documents, a System Overview and a Space Interconnections map, synthesized from the member spaces' overviews. Open a hyperspace and use the Hyperspace Overview tab to generate it. CodeKB brings each member's Space Overview up to date first, so the synthesis can take a while and shows its own token cost.
faq.impactQ: Can Agent Hopper help me assess the impact of a change?
faq.impactA: Yes. Switch Agent Hopper to Impact Analysis mode, describe the change in plain English (for example, "add input validation to all public API methods"), and the agent uses flow and dependency tracing to reason about what the change would touch.
faq.everythingQ: Is there a way to see everything at once?
faq.everythingA: Yes. The Overview page aggregates metrics across all spaces and renders a Treemap visualization of your spaces and hyperspaces, with a space-health breakdown of ready, analyzing, and failed spaces.
faq.setupQ: How do I check my deployment is set up correctly?
faq.setupA: Open Settings. It shows whether the S3 bucket, the S3 Vectors bucket, the vector index, and the git-credentials KMS key are reachable, the active Bedrock model and region, which Git providers and zip upload are enabled, and the version you are running.
faq.recreateQ: Do I need to recreate a space when the code changes?
faq.recreateA: No. For Git-sourced spaces, use "Refresh space". CodeKB diffs the latest commit against the recorded commit, re-analyzes only what changed, and atomically swaps in the updated knowledge base. Recreate only to change the source or analysis options.
faq.sizeQ: Is there a limit on repository size, and can I exclude files?
faq.sizeAPrefix: There is no hard size cap; repositories beyond 2M lines have been analyzed. CodeKB skips common noise like
faq.sizeAAuto: automatically, and you can add your own
faq.patternsA: CodeKB skips files and folders matching its exclusion patterns: the built-in defaults plus any set in CODEKB_EXCLUDE_PATTERNS_EXTRA, listed on the Settings page. A space's patterns are fixed for its lifetime: they are recorded when the space is created, and every refresh applies the same patterns. Changing the system-wide patterns affects new spaces only. To apply the current patterns to an existing repository, delete the space and create it again.
faq.multiQ: Can I search across multiple repositories at once?
faq.multiA: Yes. Use Global search across all or selected spaces, and group related spaces into a hyperspace to query them as one unit.

troubleshooting.title: Troubleshooting
troubleshooting.missingQ: Analysis finished but some files are missing.
troubleshooting.missingA: Only supported languages are analyzed; the rest are skipped and listed on the Codebase tab. Files matching the space's exclusion patterns, shown on the same tab, are not analyzed either.
troubleshooting.branchQ: My Git branch was not found.
troubleshooting.branchA: Branches and tags load from the repo once the URL is valid; pick from the list, or leave it blank for the default branch. Private repos need a saved credential first.
